standard.title: Energy Transfer and Transformation
standard.description: classify different types of energy as kinetic or potential and investigate energy transfer and transformations in simple systems
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have encountered specific energy forms across multiple years: sound energy causes vibration (AC9S2U02), heat energy transfers between objects (AC9S3U03), light travels in straight paths (AC9S5U03), electrical energy transfers in circuits (AC9S6U03). Prior learning is energy-form specific — each form was treated in isolation. The kinetic/potential classification framework, the transfer/transformation distinction, and the concept of by-product heat are all new.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students classify energy types as kinetic (movement, heat, sound, light, electrical) or potential (chemical, gravitational, elastic), distinguish energy transfer from transformation, and trace energy through multi-step systems — identifying useful outputs and by-product heat — using flow diagrams.

nodes.label: Kinetic energy — energy of active processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify kinetic energy types, explain what they share in common, and classify familiar examples.
nodes.minimum_width: Students list at least four kinetic energy types and state what they have in common.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify kinetic forms: movement/mechanical, thermal (heat), sound, light (radiant), electrical; explain that kinetic energy is associated with active motion or activity at particle or wave level; connect to prior knowledge — sound (AC9S2U02), heat (AC9S3U03), light (AC9S5U03), electrical (AC9S6U03) — now organised under one category; classify novel examples.
wider: Classify the energy types visible in a Rube Goldberg machine at different stages — identify all kinetic forms present
Investigate traditional fire-starting methods used by First Nations Australians — identify which kinetic energy forms are present at each stage

response_modes.reason: Students have met kinetic energy forms in isolation across four years. The classification step — organising familiar forms under a shared category — requires making the unifying principle (activity/motion) explicit. Without this, kinetic/potential remains two separate lists rather than a framework.

success_criteria: Names at least four kinetic energy types
Explains the shared characteristic of kinetic energy forms (associated with activity or motion)
Correctly classifies novel energy examples as kinetic

nodes.label: Potential energy — stored capacity for activity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify potential energy types, explain the stored-capacity principle, and classify familiar examples.
nodes.minimum_width: Students name at least three potential energy types and explain what distinguishes potential from kinetic energy.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify potential forms: chemical (food, fuel, batteries), gravitational (height above ground), elastic (stretched/compressed objects); explain that potential energy is stored — not currently active but capable of being released; explain that the amount of stored energy depends on position, composition or deformation; apply the classification to everyday objects; explain that potential and kinetic energy can be interconverted.
wider: Compare the energy stored in different fuels (chemical potential) — what does energy density mean and why does it matter for transport or industry?
Investigate gravitational potential energy using a ramp — how does height relate to the kinetic energy a rolling ball has at the bottom?

response_modes.reason: Potential energy is less intuitive than kinetic — 'stored' energy is not visible or directly sensed. Connecting potential to the conditions that create it (height, chemical bonds, deformation) and to the kinetic energy released when conditions change is the conceptual move that makes the category coherent.

success_criteria: Names at least three potential energy types
Explains potential energy as stored capacity — not currently active
Distinguishes potential from kinetic energy and identifies the condition that determines each

nodes.label: Energy transfer — same type, different location
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type, and give examples of thermal, mechanical and electrical transfer.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define energy transfer and give two examples of different energy types being transferred.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe transfer: heat flowing from hot to cold object (thermal transfer — same type, different location); sound passing from speaker to ear; electrical energy flowing through a circuit; a moving ball hitting a stationary ball (kinetic → kinetic); explain that in transfer, the energy type is preserved but moves from one object or location to another; contrast with transformation in preparation for N4.
wider: Investigate heat transfer through different materials — compare conductors and insulators in terms of transfer rate and explain using the particle model from AC9S7U05
Analyse sound energy transfer in a First Nations traditional instrument — how is energy transferred from player to air to listener?

response_modes.reason: Transfer and transformation are commonly confused. Transfer must be established with clear examples before transformation is introduced. The defining feature — same type, different location — needs explicit contrast with transformation (different type, same or different location) in N4.

success_criteria: Defines energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type
Gives two examples of energy transfer involving different energy types
Distinguishes a transfer event from a transformation event

nodes.label: Energy transformation — energy changing type
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another, identify common transformation sequences, and explain by-product heat.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define transformation and identify the energy type before and after in two named examples.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe common transformations: chemical → kinetic + heat (combustion); electrical → light + heat (light bulb); gravitational potential → kinetic (falling); elastic potential → kinetic + sound (stretched rubber band); explain that heat is almost always produced as a by-product in transformations — energy 'lost' to the environment; explain that by-product heat is not lost (energy conserved) but is not the useful output; connect to by-product identification in AC9S9U05 efficiency analysis.
wider: Investigate traditional fire-starting methods — trace the transformation sequence from initial stored energy (friction = mechanical → heat → chemical reaction → light + heat) and identify all by-product energy forms
Analyse a filament light bulb vs an LED: both transform electrical to light, but different proportions become by-product heat — what does this tell you about transformation efficiency?
nodes.hinge_reason: By-product heat is the conceptual foundation of efficiency analysis in AC9S9U05. Students who do not understand that heat is almost always a by-product of energy transformation — and that this reduces useful output — cannot correctly identify all outputs in an efficiency calculation or construct complete Sankey diagrams.

response_modes.reason: By-product heat requires students to extend 'energy changes type' to include unwanted outputs alongside useful ones. Students who learn transformation examples without explicitly identifying by-product heat produce systematically incomplete energy analyses in Year 9. Making by-product heat a required component of every transformation description is the scaffold.

success_criteria: Defines energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another
Identifies useful output and by-product heat in at least two named transformations
Explains that by-product heat is not lost (energy is conserved) but is not the useful output

nodes.label: Tracing energy through multi-step systems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can trace energy through a multi-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs.
nodes.minimum_width: Students trace energy through a two-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying at least one by-product.
nodes.typical_width: Students trace: roller coaster (gravitational potential → kinetic → gravitational potential → kinetic + heat + sound); Newton's cradle (kinetic → elastic potential → kinetic + heat + sound); battery torch (chemical → electrical → light + heat); First Nations fire-starting (mechanical friction → heat → combustion chemical → light + heat); identify which outputs are useful and which are by-product; explain that tracing all outputs is the prerequisite for understanding efficiency.
wider: Observe a Rube Goldberg machine and construct a complete energy trace — identify every stage, every transfer, every transformation, and every by-product
Compare energy traces for two different systems that produce the same useful output (e.g. candle vs electric light) — identify which produces more by-product heat and what this implies
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multi-step system tracing across varied contexts — mechanical, electrical, thermal, traditional technologies — is explicitly elaborated and provides genuine investigative width. Each system presents a different transformation sequence and by-product profile.

response_modes.reason: Each system context (mechanical, electrical, biological, traditional) exercises the energy tracing skill with a different sequence of types and outputs. Width here builds the generalised tracing capability the descriptor's 'investigate' demand requires.

success_criteria: Traces energy through a multi-step system naming all types at each stage
Identifies all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs in the trace
Distinguishes useful energy output from by-product outputs

nodes.label: Flow diagrams — representing and analysing energy systems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct and interpret flow diagrams representing energy through a system and use these to identify where by-product outputs occur.
nodes.minimum_width: Students construct a flow diagram for a system with at least two stages, labelling input, useful output and by-product at each stage.
nodes.typical_width: Students construct flow diagrams using arrows and labelled energy types; represent both transfers and transformations correctly; include by-products at each transformation stage; critique diagrams for completeness — are all outputs accounted for?; explain that flow diagrams are the tool for efficiency analysis in Year 9.
wider: Compare flow diagrams for electricity generation from coal and from solar — what transformation stages differ and where does by-product heat appear in each?
Critique a peer's flow diagram for completeness and accuracy — identify missing outputs or incorrectly labelled transformations

response_modes.reason: Flow diagram construction requires applying the classification (N1–N2), transfer/transformation distinction (N3–N4) and tracing skill (N5) in a representational form. Diagrams that miss by-product outputs are a systematic error that propagates into AC9S9U05's efficiency calculations. Structured practice with completeness checking is the appropriate response.

success_criteria: Constructs a flow diagram for a multi-step system with correctly labelled energy types
Includes by-product outputs at each transformation stage
Critiques a diagram for completeness — identifies any missing outputs
